title: Arrest at Lahore
hook: summoned by the emperor Jahangir's order, Guru Arjan is imprisoned and tortured in the heat of Lahore

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Adi Granth: carried into the Harmandir, with the Guru seated below it. Your line was the word has a home. Did something of yours get its proper place? Day sixty-three.

Look at the week behind you. A quiet youngest son chosen as Guru. Letters of longing from Lahore. A jealous brother. A house with four doors, a book gathered from many voices, and that book given a home. Guru Arjan has built a great deal in a short time, and people are noticing. Crowds come to Amritsar. The community is growing, organized, confident. And in 1605 a new emperor, Jahangir, takes the throne in the Mughal capital. Within a year, his order reaches the Guru. Come to Lahore. It is early summer on the plains of Punjab, the hottest time of the year. Today, the week that began in longing for Lahore ends there.
screen: `A WEEK OF BUILDING.` → `A NEW EMPEROR, JAHANGIR.` → `COME TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Why was the Guru arrested? The sources give more than one answer, and historians weigh them differently. Jahangir himself left a memoir, and in it he writes about the Guru with open irritation: too many people, Hindus and Muslims both, were following him, and the emperor wanted it stopped. There was also politics. Jahangir's own son, Prince Khusrau, had rebelled, and Jahangir's memoir itself says the prince stopped to see the Guru on his way; the Sikh accounts say the Guru blessed him, as he blessed anyone who came. And Sikh tradition adds a court official, Chandu Shah, who held a personal grudge. What the Sikh accounts agree on is what happened next. The Guru was held in Lahore, and in the heat of summer he was tortured. Tradition remembers it in terrible detail: made to sit on a red-hot iron plate, with burning sand poured over him. We won't linger on it. What Sikhs linger on is how he sat. A friend came: Mian Mir, a Muslim Sufi saint of Lahore, whom tradition remembers as close to the Guru. He was horrified, and offered to go to the emperor and plead for him. Tradition says the Guru calmly told him not to, that this too was within God's will, and that he would bear it. In the Sikh accounts, he did not shout. He did not curse the emperor. He sat, and stayed steady, and kept remembering. That word from day fourteen, simran, is doing its hardest work here. Tomorrow, how it ended, and what Sikhs call him because of it.
screen: `WHY? MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.` · `HELD IN THE HEAT OF LAHORE.` · `MIAN MIR OFFERS TO PLEAD.` · `STEADY, AND REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `STEADY IN THE HEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in stillness for one minute, and then a little longer. Nothing to fix. Nothing to answer. Let your body get still first, hands in your lap, feet on the floor. Notice anything that wants you to move: an itch, a thought, a sound. Don't fight it and don't follow it. Stay. If you remember a name for God, you can let it ride on your breath. If not, just let the breath be your anchor. The bell holds the time.
Simran. Remembering God's name, the practice Guru Arjan kept while tortured in the summer heat at Lahore, staying steady and unshouting.
Your line: steady in the heat. Today, when something gets heated, a message, a meeting, a traffic jam, take one still breath before you answer. Day sixty-three, the end of another week.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan's imprisonment and torture in Lahore in the hymns, sermons and stories of his martyrdom anniversary each summer, and the site in Lahore is marked by Gurdwara Dera Sahib.

fork.setup: you're Guru Arjan, held in the heat of Lahore. your friend Mian Mir offers to go to the emperor and plead for you. what do you say?
options: no: this too is within God's will.
tell him to raise men and break you out.
fork.reveal: tradition says the Guru calmly declined, saying he would bear what came as God's will. Sikhs remember his steadiness more than his suffering.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Lahore, the great city of Punjab where Guru Arjan was held.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Guru was arrested for breaking a law.
what it means: a growing community, a new emperor, a rebel prince, and a Guru who stayed steady while he was tortured.
what a scholar hears: Jahangir's own memoir names the Guru and his wish to end his influence, a rare case of the ruler's side writing it down.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the Khusrau meeting is not only Sikh tradition: Jahangir's own memoir records the prince stopping to see the Guru; the blessing is now attributed to the Sikh accounts. The Guru's calm is framed as the Sikh accounts' memory.
Jahangir's memoir is paraphrased (followers among Hindus and Muslims; wish to end his influence). Confirm wording and that the paraphrase is fair.
Chandu Shah's role is from Sikh tradition; some historians doubt or downplay it. Stated as 'Sikh tradition adds'. Confirm.
Torture described briefly (hot iron plate, burning sand); the cauldron is omitted to keep it non-graphic. Confirm tone.
Mian Mir's offer to intercede is tradition; the tradition that he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone is not used. Confirm.
Week-end look back covers days 57–62 (the youngest son, letters from Lahore, the jealous brother, the Harmandir, the gathering, the installation). Confirm.
